name: Windex Original
heritage_note: Blue glass cleaner since the 1930s — most families' first window spray. Formula evolved (DBC solvent era → 2-butoxyethanol → modern).

name: Formula 409
heritage_note: 'The 409' — 1960s all-purpose spray burned into muscle memory for kitchen counters.

name: Mr. Clean
heritage_note: The bald genie's cleaner, a 1950s staple that defined what 'clean' smelled like.

name: Pine-Sol
heritage_note: Pine-oil cleaner from 1929 — that 'clean pine smell' is a generational memory (and a sensitizer source).

name: Lysol All-Purpose
heritage_note: Sold since the 1889 flu era as 'household disinfectant'. Early formulas even contained cresol; generations of sickness-cleaning trust.

name: Fabuloso
heritage_note: Colgate's brightly colored multi-surface cleaner — a 1980s–90s kitchen fixture, passed down by scent loyalty.

name: Simple Green
heritage_note: The 1970s 'environmentally friendly' pioneer — one of the first green-label cleaners in ordinary homes.

name: Clorox Bleach
heritage_note: The original household disinfectant, in cupboards for 100+ years. Effective but carries respiratory + repro flags on routine indoor use.

name: Lysol Disinfectant Spray
heritage_note: The aerosol that 'kills 99.9% of germs' — a 1950s icon passed down as the default sick-day spray.

name: Lysol Toilet Bowl
heritage_note: The acid-based toilet cleaner many inherited without reading the label.

name: Scrubbing Bubbles
heritage_note: The 1970s bathroom spray that foamed 'up and at 'em' — a shower-scrub icon.

name: Comet Bathroom
heritage_note: Comet cleanser (1956) — chlorinated scouring powder era, tub rings beware.

name: Tilex Mold & Mildew
heritage_note: The bleach-based mold spray that bathrooms across two generations have reached for without gloves.

name: Soft Scrub
heritage_note: The 1968 gentle abrasive that replaced powders — 'liquid Comet', passed along as the safe scrubbing option.

name: Bar Keepers Friend
heritage_note: A stainless-steel polish from 1882 with a cult following that skipped generations entirely via word of mouth.

name: Pledge
heritage_note: Lemon-oil furniture polish (1958) — the 'clean lemon smell' of living rooms for three generations.

name: Febreze
heritage_note: Younger than the rest, but already inherited: the 'spray the couch' reflex is now a household ritual.

name: Drano Max Gel
heritage_note: Drano (1923) — the caustic drain unclogger every household inherited, lye and all.

name: Bon Ami
heritage_note: 'Hasn't scratched yet' since 1886 — the feldspar-based powder that outlived every competitor.

name: Ajax Powder
heritage_note: The 1940s scouring powder with the knight — gritty, cheap, and grandma's cabinet standby.

name: Swiffer WetJet
heritage_note: P&G's mop reinvention — the modern 'clean floor' default already being handed down.

name: Dawn Ultra
heritage_note: Dawn (1973) — the dish soap that doubles as wildlife-cleanup icon; generations trust it on their greasiest pots.

name: Palmolive
heritage_note: A brand since 1898 — 'Palmolive' dish liquid is literally a great-grandparent's soap.

name: Tide
heritage_note: The 1946 laundry breakthrough that became the default 'family detergent' for 80 years.

name: 20 Mule Team Borax (BMVC)
heritage_note: Mined in Death Valley and hauled by 20-mule teams since 1891 — the all-purpose laundry booster grandma swore by. Still in most US grocery aisles; restricted across the EU for reproductive toxicity.

name: Zud Heavy Duty Cleanser
heritage_note: Powdered rust remover since mid-20th century — go-to for tough rust stains on porcelain, tile, and metal. "The rust remover your grandmother used."

name: Murphy Oil Soap
heritage_note: Original oil soap formula since 1905 — generations of wood furniture care. Potassium oleate (plant-oil soap) base, not petroleum solvent.

name: Cascade Complete ActionPacs
ings: Copolymer of Acrylic Maleic and Sulphonic Acids
heritage_note: Cascade launched 1953 as the first synthetic dishwasher detergent — generations have trusted it to clean dishes without pre-rinse.

name: Biokleen Bac-Out Stain & Odor Eliminator
note: Enzymatic odor eliminator — STR-relevant for pet/organic odors. SDS discloses full list incl. CAS numbers; microbial mixture has no CAS (biological).

name: Puracy Natural Multi-Surface Cleaner (Green Tea & Lime)
source: Manufacturer full ingredient disclosure (puracy.com product page + ingredients page)
note: Plant-based multi-surface spray. Fragrance allergens (limonene, linalool, geraniol) disclosed — EU allergen-style transparency.

name: Better Life What-Ever All-Purpose Cleaner (Unscented)
source: Manufacturer label disclosure (multiple retailers incl. Leaping Bunny listed ingredients)
note: Plant-derived surfactants, unscented. Preservative methylisothiazolinone <0.01% — a known sensitizer at larger concentrations.

name: Granite Gold Daily Cleaner
source: Manufacturer SDS (Granite Gold Inc., San Diego) — Home Depot-hosted PDF, Section 3 composition
note: Newer manufacturer SDS lists 'proprietary ingredients 1-10%' — partial disclosure flag: the 5 named ingredients are from the earlier full SDS; current formula may differ. Mountain-relevant: granite/stone counter care.

name: Resolve Heavy Traffic Foam Carpet Cleaner
note: US formulation. SmartLabel also discloses fragrance components Butylphenyl Methylpropional, Dipropylene Glycol and Eugenol, and non-functional constituents (ethane, isopentane, pentane, acrylic acid, methyl methacrylate, DEGBE). Preserved by the CMIT/MIT pair — the allergen headline here.

name: Krud Kutter Original Cleaner & Degreaser
note: Concentrated alkaline degreaser, pH <12.2 (manufacturer TDS), 0% VOC. TDS describes the surfactant blend only as 'proprietary blend of biodegradable surfactants' — ingredient identity is taken from the SDS Section 3 hazardous-substances block, which lists only the classified components. Incomplete-by-design disclosure; noted rather than padded.

name: Weiman Stainless Steel Cleaner & Polish
note: Mineral-oil polish in an LPG aerosol. Manufacturer's own ingredient list; the SDS marks mineral oil 10-30% with exact concentrations withheld as trade secret. Product-level aspiration hazard (H304) comes from the mineral oil / distillate fraction.

name: LA's Totally Awesome All-Purpose Cleaner
source: Manufacturer MSDS + retail composition listing (Awesome Products)
note: Sourcing caveat: the manufacturer page markets the formula but does not enumerate ingredients. Composition taken from a retail listing of the current formulation (Butyl Carbitol = DEGBE; Ecosurf EH-9 = an alcohol ethoxylate, recorded under the existing 'Ethoxylated Alcohol' entry) plus the manufacturer's 2011 MSDS (which additionally listed an orange-oil blend, no longer shown). Weaker disclosure than the other three adds; flagged rather than presented as equivalent.

name: Clorox Disinfecting Wipes, Fresh Scent
note: EPA-registered disinfecting wipe (EPA Reg. 5813-79). Two BAC-type quats are the actives; the SDS lists each at ~0.184% by weight. SmartLabel flags hexoxyethanol, isopropanol and the C12-18 quat on California SB258 designated lists. The C12-14 and C12-18 quats are UVCBs with no discrete PubChem CID, recorded extrapolated by class.

name: OxiClean Versatile Stain Remover
note: Oxygen-bleach stain remover. SDS composition: sodium carbonate 50-75%, sodium percarbonate 30-45%, ethoxylated alcohol 1-3%, sodium polycarboxylate 1%, sodium metasilicate 1%. Two SDS revisions name the surfactant differently (C12-16 vs C12-15 ethoxylated) — recorded under the existing generic 'Ethoxylated Alcohol' entry rather than over-precise. The manufacturer states the product 'contains a light fragrance' but the SDS does not enumerate it; noted rather than padded.

name: Woolite Delicates Laundry Detergent
note: Hand-wash/delicates detergent. SmartLabel discloses five fragrance components individually (butylphenyl methylpropional, dipropylene glycol, eugenol, hexyl salicylate, isoeugenol) — included here per the DB's fragrance-allergen pattern. Butylphenyl methylpropional (Lilial) is the headline: an EU-banned CMR still disclosed in a US product. Preserved with the BIT/MIT pair.

name: Mr. Clean Magic Eraser
source: P&G SDS (composition section, reproduced in university chemical-safety listing)
note: Melamine-formaldehyde abrasive foam. P&G's SDS classifies the finished product 'Not Classified' with no hazardous ingredients listed, and notes it is treated as an article under TSCA. The single disclosed component is a melamine-formaldehyde copolymer (formaldehyde is a known decomposition product under heat/fire). One-ingredient product — recorded as-is rather than padded.

name: Persil ProClean Liquid Laundry Detergent, Intense Fresh
ings: Fatty Acids, C8-18 and C18-Unsaturated Sodium Salts
note: Mainstream US liquid detergent. SmartLabel flags propylene glycol, polyethyleneimine alkoxylate, Fragrance, protease, amylase and cellulase with the DL symbol (California Cleaning Products Right to Know designated lists / EU Annex III fragrance allergens). Sodium metaborate is the borate enzyme stabilizer — the same boron chemistry the EU classifies as reproductive toxicant 1B while US products sell it off the shelf. Henkel discloses the enzyme as 'Protease enzyme'; recorded here under the existing 'Subtilisin' entry (the protease used in detergents).

name: Clorox Clean-Up All Purpose Cleaner with Bleach, Original
source: Clorox SmartLabel public ingredient disclosure (updated 11/19/2024); SDS EPA Reg. 5813-21
note: EPA-registered disinfecting bleach spray (EPA Reg. 5813-21; SDS lists sodium hypochlorite 1-5%, sodium hydroxide 0.1-1%). Two notable disclosures on a mainstream bleach cleaner: benzophenone — prohibited in EU cosmetics (Annex II, Entry 1703) and DL-flagged on this label — and sodium chlorate, the oxidizer that accumulates as hypochlorite decays in storage.

name: Spic and Span All-Purpose Disinfecting Spray and Glass Cleaner
source: Church & Dwight SDS (concentrate, 5/14/2018) + retail ingredient disclosure
note: Disinfecting all-purpose / glass cleaner (concentrate). SDS composition ranges: butoxydiglycol (DEGBE) 10-30%, 2-hexyloxyethanol 5-10%, 1-amino-2-propanol 5-10%, decyl octyl glucosides 1-5%. The retail disclosure additionally lists the two quat actives and a long fragrance accord (limonene, linalool, citral, coumarin, geraniol, hexyl cinnamal, benzyl salicylate, benzyl acetate, ionone, p-cymene, phenethyl alcohol, terpineol, orange oil terpenes, dipropylene glycol) — recorded here as the generic 'Fragrance' entry rather than enumerating every scent note, matching house convention. Butoxydiglycol is recorded under the existing 'Diethylene Glycol Monobutyl Ether' entry (same compound, CAS 112-34-5).

name: Downy Ultra Free & Gentle Liquid Fabric Conditioner
note: Marketed as dye-free and perfume-free and accepted by the National Eczema Association, yet the SmartLabel disclosure still lists a 'Fragrance Ingredient' — recorded here under the existing 'Fragrance' entry, with the literal disclosure wording noted. The softener active is the ester-quat DEEDMAC, disclosed without a percentage.
